specPoints.text: understand how resistance to antibiotics can increase in bacterial populations, and appreciate how such an increase can lead to infections being difficult to control

primer.text: When doctors reach for an antibiotic, they are running a live selection experiment. This note follows a single random mutation that shields one bacterium from a drug, and shows how treatment itself promotes the descendants of that lucky cell until a resistant strain dominates and combination therapy becomes the only option left.

lessons.title: How Resistance Rises in a Population
lessons.opening: A random mutation can hand a bacterium an allele that shields it from an antibiotic; once the drug is applied, only the carriers survive, reproduce and spread that shield, so the resistance version grows more common generation after generation until the whole strain shrugs the drug off.
keyPoints: Mutations arise at random and can create an allele conferring antibiotic resistance.
Exposure to the drug kills bacteria without the resistance allele.
Survivors reproduce, handing the protective allele to their offspring.
Over generations the resistance allele rises in frequency, producing a resistant strain.
Resistant infections may need a different antibiotic, or several at once.

low.restatement: The drug wipes out the undefended bacteria, and the defended ones multiply in the space left behind.
low.analogy: A flood that only strong swimmers survive: the next generation is built entirely from strong swimmers.
low.examPointer: Always include the four stages: variation, survival, reproduction, rising allele frequency.

medium.restatement: Selection does not create the allele; it filters the population, so the pre-existing resistant version dominates after treatment.
medium.analogy: The antibiotic is a sieve, not a sculptor: it chooses among existing variants rather than designing new ones.
medium.examPointer: If asked why resistance spreads, say carriers reproduce more, not that bacteria learn or adapt on purpose.

check.stem: What event first creates the resistance allele in a bacterial population?

options.text: A random mutation in the genetic material
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Exposure to the antibiotic creates it
options.explanation: The drug only selects among existing variants; the allele must already exist.

options.text: The patient's immune system designs it
options.explanation: Immunity and bacterial genetics are separate systems.

options.text: Resistant bacteria invade from elsewhere
options.explanation: The taught account starts the allele with mutation inside the population.

check.stem: What happens to bacteria lacking the resistance allele when the antibiotic is applied?

options.text: They die, leaving the resistant carriers to thrive
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: They mutate immediately and survive
options.explanation: Mutation is random and does not answer the drug on demand.

options.text: They become dormant forever
options.explanation: The taught outcome is death of the undefended cells.

options.text: They switch to a different antibiotic
options.explanation: Individual bacteria cannot swap their own treatment.

check.stem: Why does the resistance allele become more common over generations?

options.text: Carriers reproduce more successfully and pass the allele on
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The allele grows stronger inside each cell
options.explanation: Frequency rises through inheritance, not internal strengthening.

options.text: Bacteria purposefully evolve to survive
options.explanation: Selection acts on existing variation without intent.

options.text: The drug breeds resistance into survivors
options.explanation: The drug filters; it does not breed anything.

check.stem: Which process does antibiotic resistance exemplify?

options.text: Natural selection
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Genetic engineering
options.explanation: No laboratory intervenes in the taught account.

options.text: Active transport
options.explanation: That moves molecules across membranes, not populations.

options.text: Mitosis
options.explanation: Cell division alone does not explain the changing allele frequency.

check.stem: A resistant infection fails to respond to its usual drug. What is the treatment implication?

options.text: A different antibiotic, sometimes several combined, must be used
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The same drug at a higher dose always works
options.explanation: Resistance can defeat the usual drug outright.

options.text: No treatment is possible
options.explanation: Other antibiotics remain options.

options.text: The infection must simply run its course untreated
options.explanation: The taught account prescribes alternative drugs.

check.stem: List the four stages that describe how antibiotic resistance spreads through a population.
check.modelAnswer: Mutation produces the resistance allele, the antibiotic kills non-carriers, surviving carriers reproduce and pass the allele on, and the allele frequency increases each generation.

check.stem: State why antibiotic resistance makes infections harder to control.
check.modelAnswer: Resistant bacteria survive the usual drugs, so treatment needs a different antibiotic or several together.

check.stem: Explain why using an antibiotic does not create resistance, even though resistance rises after treatment.
check.modelAnswer: The resistance allele already exists through random mutation; the drug acts by natural selection, killing non-carriers, so the frequency increases rather than the drug instructing bacteria to change.

check.stem: A patient stops a course of antibiotics early. Describe how this can raise the frequency of resistant bacteria remaining in the body.
check.modelAnswer: Surviving bacteria include any carrying resistance alleles; with the drug gone they reproduce freely, so the resistant forms multiply and their allele frequency climbs in the population left behind.

glossary.definition: A drug that kills bacteria or stops them growing.
A gene version that lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic.
The process in which better-suited individuals survive and breed more.
A bacterial population descended from one type, here a drug-resistant one.
